transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-02-02 16:00 PST | Duration 62m | Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Lina Cho (Redwood CSM); Kevin Tran, Priya Shah, Marcus Lee, Sofia Romero (Auric)

Summary section (auto): Quick mapping of Auric's latency SLOs (p95 300-500ms target for short chat flows), discussion of token/sec benchmarks and batching economics, and Private/VPC security expectations.

[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood Inference, with Diego our systems engineer and Lina on CS. Kevin, Marcus, thanks for the time. Could you kick off with what you're trying to achieve?

[00:22] Kevin (Head of ML): Yeah thanks, um quick context — Auric runs a customer-facing summarization chat and a multi-turn RAG assistant, average request length maybe 80 tokens in prompt, generation 120 tokens on average. Our p95 latency target for interactive flows is around 350ms for most small-chat endpoints, but we also have longer analytic jobs that can tolerate seconds.

[00:45] Priya (Platform): And important: we expect bursty traffic, think product launches — concurrency can jump from 50 to 800 sessions in minutes. We need clarity on warmup, cold starts, and how Redwood does autoscaling on Dedicated vs Hosted.

[01:10] Diego (SE): OK got it. A few quick clarifying qs — is your traffic mostly streaming token-by-token to the client, or do you buffer and return full output?

[01:22] Marcus (CTO): Streaming for chat UI yes, we stream to the browser. For batch summarization we return full payloads. Streaming is primary for the interactive SLOs.

[01:38] Diego (SE): Good. Streaming adds tail-latency considerations because each token must hit the model with low inter-token delay. For p95 350ms we need to look at model choice, token/sec throughput, batching, and whether you use prefix/KV cache. Do you cache user contexts?

[01:57] Kevin: We do a lightweight session cache on our side but not prefix caching at model-level. We've been worried about KV-cash behavior — we typed cash but mean cache — I think our ops term is 'session cache' at app layer. Curious about Redwood's KV cache and warm KV reuse across requests.

[02:25] Diego (SE): Redwood's runtime supports KV cache reuse when you pin model variants and reuse the same generation path; that reduces tokens/sec work for repeated context. In Hosted we do automatic prefix caching and short-lived cache entries; Dedicated gives you more control over cache eviction. In Private you bring your own infra so cache persistence depends on your deployment config.

[02:50] Priya: For compliance we need SOC2 Type II, SAML SSO, enterprise KMS support and audit logs. Also VPC peering for Private.

[03:05] Lina (CSM): We'll send the SOC2 + ISO artifacts and a sample network diagram after.

[03:15] Maya: Good. On the perf numbers — you mentioned concurrency spikes to 800. What's the steady-state concurrency and peak token/sec expectation?

[03:30] Kevin: Steady-state around 120 concurrent streams, peaks ~800 for minutes. Average tokens/sec per stream about 10-15 tokens/sec, but when users paste long prompts it jumps. So safe planning number is ~1.5M tokens per minute at peak, but that's with many assumptions.

[03:55] Diego: OK, to translate: 1.5M tokens/min is roughly 25k tokens/sec across cluster. For streaming p95 350ms on a 70B-class model is tight unless you do quantization and smaller model variants for tail. What's your model preference? Open weights or customer-provided?

[04:15] Kevin: We prefer open models for cost, currently prototyping on a 13B and a 70B open family for fidelity tests. For production we might use a mixed approach: 13B for short-chat and 70B for high-quality summarization.

[04:32] Diego (SE): That's common. For 13B streaming at <350ms p95 you can get there with compact batching and tuned kernels. 70B needs more GPUs and specialized kernels — Redwood Dedicated can reserve GPU pools with lower tail latency and predictable throughput. Hosted is variable but we provide perf profiles.

[05:00] Priya: How do you measure p95 in your reports? Is it end-to-end (client to client) or model-only?

[05:12] Diego: We provide both. Our p95 model-side is model-serve latency; we also produce token-level latency and client-facing p95 which includes network and SDK overhead. Usually we show both and provide breakdown in the Console.

[05:32] Marcus: For our SLOs we want end-to-end. If Redwood can get model p95 below 200ms consistently we can meet 350ms E2E.

[05:45] Diego: Makes sense. We should run a token/sec bench using your sample prompts and traffic profile. I recommend a 48-hour run that includes cold-start cycles to capture variance.

[06:00] Kevin: Sounds good. What's the expected delta between Hosted and Dedicated in those runs?

[06:10] Diego: Hosted typically has slightly higher variance and a higher median latency because resources are multiplexed, but for many customers the median is acceptable. Dedicated gives you pinned GPU pools, lower variance — p95 improvements of ~15-40% depending on workload. Private depends — if you can provide fast interconnect and GPUs we can match Dedicated behavior but you manage infra and kernel compatibility (CUDA/ROCm).

[06:40] Sofia (SRE): On the Private side we need HSM/KMS integration for keys and detailed audit logs. Also curious about fallback behavior: if your Dedicated pool is saturated does Redwood auto-fallback to a smaller model?

[06:55] Diego: Yes, we have policy-based routing and automatic fallbacks to compatible model variants (for example, from 70B float to quantized 70B or to 13B) depending on latency and capacity policies you configure. Fallbacks can be synchronous or asynchronous with a degraded-quality signal.

[07:20] Priya: What about batching — does streaming hurt batching efficiency?

[07:28] Diego: Streaming reduces traditional large batch opportunities because tokens are emitted sooner, but our continuous batching works across in-flight tokens and can batch micro-batches to improve throughput without increasing inter-token delay much. It's workload-dependent.

[07:52] Kevin: We also care about memory footprint — how many requests per GPU for the 13B and 70B quantized paths?

[08:05] Diego: Rough rule: optimized quantized 13B can support dozens of concurrent streams per A100/P4-like GPU with continuous batching; 70B quantized on A100x2 shapes fewer — maybe low double-digits depending on sequence length and KV cache size. We'll include conservative numbers in the perf sheet.

[08:35] Marcus: Pricing will be key. We want a clear trade-off: cost per 1k tokens for Hosted vs price for Dedicated reservation + utilization assumptions.

[08:48] Maya: We'll provide a pricing baseline after we run the bench; Dedicated pricing includes reserved GPU-hour commitments and burst options. We'll share a model for expected unit economics.

[09:05] Kevin: Can Redwood attach tracing per request so we can see token-level timing?

[09:15] Diego: Yes, Console provides per-request traces and token-timers — we can instrument traces to show kernel time vs queue time vs serialization. We can also push tracing hooks to your observability stack.

[09:35] Priya: A question on cold starts: if you scale from 50 to 800, how fast do new rigs spin up? Do Dedicated pools pre-warm?

[09:46] Diego: Autoscaling speed depends on the pool config. Dedicated pools can keep warm standby capacity to handle bursts; you set min active and min warm nodes. Hosted uses a multi-tenant cold-start mitigation layer and fast cold-launch paths, but worst-case cold starts can add 300-800ms depending on the model. We always recommend pre-warm windows for predictable p95.

[10:18] Marcus: On the quantization note, do you advise 4-bit quant for 70B in production? We worry about quality regressions.

[10:27] Diego: 4-bit PTQ or QLoRA style quantization can work for many tasks, but we recommend running evals against your prompt set. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles per workload and flag quality regressions in evals.

[10:50] Kevin: Great. Ok can we sketch an initial benchmark plan now?

[11:00] Diego: Plan: 1) Auric provides sample prompt set, traffic trace, and target SLOs. 2) Redwood runs a 48h bench across Hosted and Dedicated-like configs: a) 13B endpoint, b) 70B quantized, c) 70B full float if you want high-fidelity. Each run will include steady-state and injected bursts, cold-start cycles, and streaming latency measurement. We'll capture tokens/sec, per-token latency distribution, p95 E2E and model-only, and resource utilization.

[11:35] Priya: We'll assemble prompt set and send by 2026-02-03. Any sample format?

[11:43] Diego: CSV of prompts + metadata (sequence lengths, expected streaming behavior) is fine. Also include a traffic trace or arrival distribution. We'll give a template.

[11:55] Maya: For security, we'll attach SOC2 artifacts and network diagram. Private deployment questions will require deeper ops sync.

[12:05] Marcus: If the benchmark shows Hosted meets our p95 we might avoid Dedicated. If not, we'll look at Dedicated reservation. We want an ROI calc before committing.

[12:20] Lina: We'll include a simple cost model to compare Hosted vs Dedicated utilization at different traffic shapes.

[12:30] Kevin: Are there any gotchas around GPU driver versions for Private? We run ROCm clusters in EMEA.

[12:40] Diego: Good callout. Private deployments must match driver/ROCm/CUDA compat. Some kernels require specific CUDA versions for optimal perf; we'll validate compatibility in the ops workshop.

[12:58] Priya: One more Q: audit logs retention and export — can we push logs to our SIEM?

[13:05] Lina: Yes, we support log export to S3 and to SIEM via secure forwarders; retention configurable in Enterprise plans.

[13:20] Kevin: Cool. Any immediate blockers?

[13:25] Maya: Not yet. We'll do the bench, share pricing, and run an ops workshop for Private if you want to pursue that path.

[13:40] Diego: I'll also sketch a benchmark harness and example config for burst injection and streaming measurement.

[13:50] Marcus: Let's talk timeline — we want results within two weeks ideally.

[13:56] Diego: A first-pass bench (Hosted + 13B) can be done in 48-72 hours after prompts. Full matrix including Dedicated and 70B will be about 10 business days.

[14:18] Priya: Sounds acceptable.

[14:25] -- Recap / Next steps --
- Maya: Redwood to run benchmark once prompts and traffic trace received (48h for first pass).
- Maya: Send SOC2/ISO + network diagram.
- Diego: Share bench harness config and perf spreadsheet.
- Priya: Provide prompts and traffic traces by 2026-02-03.

[14:55] Action items restated: Maya to email perf spreadsheet; Diego to run bench after receipt; Priya to send sample data.

[15:10] Kevin: Thanks everyone, appreciate the thoroughness.

[15:20] Maya: Thanks, talk soon.

[61:45] Meeting end.

Notes: Transcript includes occasional mis-hearings ("KV cash"->cache, model names sometimes lowercase). References to Redwood Dedicated as "Dedicate" in automated transcription. Links referenced: Perf sheet (link sent in follow-up), SOC2 artifact pack (link), bench harness repo (link).
